summary: Describes LISP+ALT, an experimental distributed index system that helps a LISP Ingress Tunnel Router or Map-Resolver find the Egress Tunnel Router holding the mapping for a given endpoint identifier. The resolver can then ask that router for the actual locator list.

plainLanguage.summary: LISP+ALT helps a router find which Egress Tunnel Router has a mapping for a destination. The overlay routes the request but does not carry the mapping itself.

questions: how does lisp find the router that holds a mapping
does lisp alt carry eid to rloc mappings
subtitle: A BGP-based overlay that routes LISP mapping requests to the ETR holding an EID mapping.

tldr.problem: A LISP router needs a way to find which Egress Tunnel Router holds the mapping for an Endpoint Identifier.
tldr.mechanism: The Alternative Logical Topology uses tunnels and BGP to propagate EID-prefix routes, then forwards Map-Requests toward the router that holds the mapping.
tldr.outcome: The ALT carries paths to mapping holders, not the EID-to-RLOC mappings themselves. RFC 6836 is Experimental and identifies open deployment questions.

facts.label: Mapping reply
facts.value: Sent by the ETR holding the mapping

today: RFC 6836 is an Experimental specification published for examination, implementation, and evaluation. The RFC itself says that the best ALT design and operational model still need further experience.

sections.title: The Alternative Logical Topology
sections.content:
The Alternative Logical Topology (ALT) is a distributed index for Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP). An Ingress Tunnel Router or Map-Resolver uses it to find the Egress Tunnel Router that holds a mapping for an Endpoint Identifier.

ALT-Routers form an overlay using tunnels and BGP. They exchange EID-prefix reachability information and forward requests toward the router that originated the route. The ALT does not distribute EID-to-RLOC mapping data; the ETR returns that data in a Map-Reply.
sections.plainLanguage: The ALT routes a mapping request to the router responsible for an EID-prefix. That router sends the actual locator information back in a reply.

sections.title: Map-Requests and Data-Probes
sections.content:
An ITR can send a Map-Request into the ALT when it needs an EID-to-RLOC mapping. The ALT forwards the request using its EID-prefix routes, and the ETR that holds the mapping answers with a Map-Reply. The reply normally travels over the ordinary Internet to an ITR RLOC, not through the ALT.

The RFC also describes a Data-Probe, which carries an initial data packet through the ALT while requesting a mapping. It is not recommended for normal use because a tunneled overlay may not handle heavy data traffic; the RFC says it should be enabled only for experiments.
sections.plainLanguage: A Map-Request asks where an EID can be reached, and the ETR replies with RLOC information. A Data-Probe also carries data, but the RFC discourages its use outside experiments.

sections.title: Tunnels and BGP Between ALT-Routers
sections.content:
The ALT is a roughly hierarchical, partial mesh of links between ALT-Routers. The specification uses GRE tunnels and runs BGP over them. Each ALT-Router acts as an Autonomous System hop; the BGP path helps choose a route and avoid loops.

Because the next hops are tunnel interfaces, the RFC says an Interior Gateway Protocol is not needed to resolve those next hops. It recommends keeping ALT-Routers logically and physically separate from routers that carry native Internet traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: ALT-Routers exchange routes over tunnels. The tunnels form a separate overlay that carries mapping requests across the Internet.

sections.title: Connecting Sites to the ALT
sections.content:
An ETR can register EID-prefixes with a Map-Server, use a static route on an edge ALT-Router, or connect directly to the ALT with a tunnel and BGP. The RFC expects Map-Server registration to be the common approach.

An ITR can send requests through a Map-Resolver, use an ALT default route, or connect directly to an ALT-Router. The Map-Resolver route is expected to be the common approach. Once an ITR learns a mapping, it can send later packets directly to an RLOC until the mapping expires.
sections.plainLanguage: Most sites can use a Map-Server to register and a Map-Resolver to send requests. After learning a mapping, an ITR sends later packets directly to a Locator.

sections.title: Route Aggregation and Security
sections.content:
ALT-Routers aggregate EID-prefixes to reduce route information. An ALT-Router should generate an aggregate only when it can learn the state of all more-specific prefixes that make it up. The RFC describes safeguards for holes in an aggregate, where a destination might not belong to a LISP site.

The security discussion lists risks such as false mappings, denial of service, reconnaissance, and leaking EID-prefixes into global routing. Suggested protections include explicit peering, protected BGP connections, message nonces, and rate limiting. The RFC also says further experience is needed to determine the best way to build and operate the ALT.
sections.plainLanguage: Route aggregation works only when a router knows the component prefixes well enough to handle missing destinations. The RFC also identifies security and operational questions that require experience.
